composing_text: 7th Canadian Infantry Brigade; 8th Canadian Infantry Brigade; 9th Canadian Infantry Brigade
current_activity: assaulting Juno Beach and advancing inland toward Caen
notes: Landed at Juno (Courseulles area); advanced inland; stopped short of Caen by 21st Panzer Division.

current_activity: facing the 12th SS Panzer Division on the Caen-Bayeux road
notes: 12th SS Panzer Division recon battalion committed 7 June and by 8 June 12th SS held the Caen-Bayeux road between Authie and Carpiquet (R449 p. 347-348), on the line that the 3rd Canadian Division was to reach from Juno (R013). [Review (V-007): neither cited source describes the division in an attack on 8 June; the activity and the event type attack are inferred from that position. The activity wording no longer says the division was contained.]

current_activity: attacking Le Mesnil-Patry; costly failure
notes: Queen's Own Rifles of Canada and 1st Hussars attacked Le Mesnil-Patry 11 June in support of 50th Division; a costly failure.

current_activity: Operation Windsor: 8th Brigade takes Carpiquet village and the north hangars, a partial victory
notes: Event date: 4 July 1944 (Stacey, p. 153). Event definition: The 8th Infantry Brigade, with The Royal Winnipeg Rifles attached, attacks Carpiquet village and airfield (Operation Windsor) under the 1st British Corps; the village and the northern hangars are taken but the south hangars and control buildings stay in enemy hands (p. 155). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 153: "the attack was delivered on the morning of 4 July"; "The attack was to be made by the 8th Infantry Brigade"; p. 155: "The day's work had thus been only a partial victory"; "We now held Carpiquet village and the northern hangars". Location: Carpiquet, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Carpiquet village and its airfield as the objective (p. 153). Commander: Maj.-Gen. R. F. L. Keller (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: to 8 Aug. 44). Opponents: 12th SS Panzer Division (Stacey, p. 153).

current_activity: Enters Caen: Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders first in; 8th Brigade holds Carpiquet airfield
notes: Event date: 9 July 1944 (Stacey, p. 162). Event definition: On the second day of Operation Charnwood the 9th Brigade enters Caen, the Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders first, and the 8th Brigade completes the occupation of Carpiquet airfield; Stacey says Caen was then in Allied hands, 33 days later than planned (p. 162). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 162: "The Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders were the first battalion to enter the city"; "had completed the occupation of Carpiquet airfield"; "Caen was in Allied hands". Location: Caen, Calvados with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names the centre of Caen as reached by the 9th Brigade at 13:35 (p. 162). Commander: Maj.-Gen. R. F. L. Keller (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: to 8 Aug. 44).

current_activity: Passes from I Corps to II Canadian Corps at 15:00 when the corps takes over the Caen front
notes: Event date: 11 July 1944, 15:00 (Stacey, p. 166). Event definition: The division, which had been under the 1st British Corps (I Corps) since D Day, comes under II Canadian Corps at 15:00 on 11 July when the corps takes over about 8000 yards of the Caen front. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 153: "It was still under the 1st British Corps"; p. 166: "At 3:00 p.m. on 11 July it took over about 8000 yards of front in the Caen sector; with the 2nd and 3rd Canadian Infantry Divisions, the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade and the 2nd Canadian 60 Army Group Royal Artillery under command". Location: Caen sector (existing area place PL0059) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the existing area place and stands for the divisional sector. Location support: Stacey names the Caen sector (p. 166); the division held the line north-west of Caen before 9 July (p. 153). Commander: Maj.-Gen. R. F. L. Keller (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: to 8 Aug. 44).

current_activity: Operation Atlantic: 8th Brigade fights through Colombelles steelworks and Giberville, 9th Brigade into Vaucelles
notes: Event date: 18 July 1944 (Stacey, pp. 171-172). Event definition: The 8th Brigade crosses the start line about 08:00 east of the Orne and fights through the Colombelles chateau and steelworks and Giberville, while the 9th Brigade passes it and by midnight is in the eastern part of Vaucelles (pp. 171-172). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 171: "capturing Colombelles, Giberville and Mondeville"; p. 172: "The North Shore was to clear the steelworks"; "the Queen's Own completed the clearing of Giberville". Location: Colombelles, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Colombelles and its steelworks as the brigade objective (pp. 171-172). Commander: Maj.-Gen. R. F. L. Keller (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: to 8 Aug. 44).

current_activity: Operation Spring: North Nova Scotia Highlanders attack Tilly-la-Campagne but cannot clear it
notes: Event date: 25 July 1944 (Stacey, p. 189). Event definition: On the 3rd Division front The North Nova Scotia Highlanders attack Tilly-la-Campagne in the dark and get a foothold in the village but cannot clear it (p. 189). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 189: "The North Nova Scotia Highlanders attacked Tilly-la-Campagne with three companies forward"; "they could not clear the place". Location: Tilly-la-Campagne, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Tilly-la-Campagne as the objective (p. 189). Commander: Maj.-Gen. R. F. L. Keller (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: to 8 Aug. 44).

current_activity: Relieved by 4th Armoured Division at 04:30 after 55 days in the line; withdraws for a short rest
notes: Event date: 31 July 1944, 04:30 (Stacey, p. 202). Event definition: The 4th Canadian Armoured Division relieves the 3rd Division in the line; the 3rd Division withdraws to the vicinity of Colomby-sur-Thaon for a short rest after 55 days in the face of the enemy. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 202: "It relieved the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division, which after 55 days in the face of the enemy"; "The relief was completed at 4:30 a.m. on 31 July". Location: Colomby-sur-Thaon, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: Stacey says the division withdrew to the vicinity of the village, not to the village itself. Location support: Stacey names the vicinity of Colomby-sur-Thaon as the rest area (p. 202). Commander: Maj.-Gen. R. F. L. Keller (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: to 8 Aug. 44).

current_activity: General Keller wounded when Allied bombers hit divisional tactical headquarters; Blackader takes over
notes: Event date: 8 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 224). Event definition: During Operation Totalize Allied bombing hits the tactical headquarters of the division and the divisional commander is wounded and evacuated; the 8th Brigade commander takes the division temporarily (p. 224). Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry takes the division on 18 August (Appendix G). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 224: "Major-General R. F. L. Keller, the divisional commander, was wounded and evacuated"; "Brigadier Blackader of the 8th Brigade took over the division temporarily". Location: Caen, Calvados with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is a representative one for the divisional area, not a headquarters position. Location support: Stacey does not give the position of the divisional tactical headquarters; it is placed in the Caen area, where the corps was assembled for the attack (p. 223 puts one bombing error near Caen). Commander: Brig. J. M. Blackader, the 8th Brigade commander, who took the division temporarily after Keller was wounded on 8 August (Stacey, pp. 224 and 230).

current_activity: Operation Tractable: division crosses the Laison valley; 1st Hussars cross at Rouvres, North Shore take Sassy
notes: Event date: 14 August 1944 (Stacey, pp. 239-241). Event definition: The 3rd Division column on the right of the corps, headed by the 2nd Armoured Brigade with flails, then the 7th Reconnaissance Regiment and the 9th Brigade in carriers, crosses the Laison valley, a squadron of the 1st Hussars finding a crossing at Rouvres, and by night the 8th Brigade has cleared its part of the valley and the North Shore Regiment is in Sassy (p. 241). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 239: "The 3rd Division column, on the right, was headed by the tanks of the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade"; p. 241: "the reserve squadron discovered a crossing at Rouvres"; "the North Shore Regiment had occupied Sassy". Location: Rouvres, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Rouvres as the crossing found by the reserve squadron of the 1st Hussars (p. 241). Commander: Brig. J. M. Blackader, the 8th Brigade commander, who took the division temporarily after Keller was wounded on 8 August (Stacey, pp. 224 and 230).

current_activity: Canadian Scottish take Point 168 north of Falaise in a costly afternoon attack; 7th Brigade on Point 159 next day
notes: Event date: 15 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 249). Event definition: On the second day of the advance towards Falaise the 1st Canadian Scottish Regiment, under the 2nd Armoured Brigade, takes Point 168 east of the Falaise road with its heaviest casualties of the campaign so far; on 16 August the 7th Brigade is on the high ground about Point 159 (p. 250). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 249: "On the ridge immediately east of the Falaise Road the 1st Battalion Canadian Scottish Regiment, fighting under command of the 2nd Armoured Brigade, and supported by the 1st Hussars, met and beat down tenacious opposition on Point 168"; p. 250: "Meanwhile the 3rd Division had pushed south from Point 168 and the 7th Brigade occupied the high ground about Point 159"; p. 248: "On the morning of the 15th our advance towards Falaise was resumed". Location: Falaise, Calvados (north of the town) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: Point 168 is a map height a few miles north of Falaise; the point is the town of Falaise and stands for the area, with a wider precision. Location support: Stacey names Point 168, a height east of the Falaise road, and does not give a village; Point 159 is described as the southern butt of the ridge above Versainville (p. 249). Commander: Brig. J. M. Blackader, the 8th Brigade commander, who took the division temporarily after Keller was wounded on 8 August (Stacey, pp. 224 and 230).

current_activity: Moves up through the Dives valley to hold the east bank of the Dives from Morteaux-Couliboeuf to Trun
notes: Event date: 18 August 1944 (Stacey, pp. 256 and 259). Event definition: Simonds orders the division, now under Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry, to hold the east bank of the Dives from Morteaux-Couliboeuf to Trun; the leading 7th Brigade is north-west of Trun by evening. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 259: "On the afternoon of the 18th General Simonds had ordered the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division (which Major-General D. C. Spry had now taken over) to move up and hold the east bank of the Dives from Morteaux-Couliboeuf to Trun"; p. 256: "by the evening of 18 August the 7th Infantry Brigade, leading its advance, was in the area immediately". Location: Trun, Orne with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the division held a line along the river; the point is Trun, the southern end of it. Location support: Stacey names Trun as the end of the line to be held and places the leading brigade north-west of it (p. 256). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: 9th Brigade beats off a German attack at Magny and meets the 53rd Division about Trun as the Gap closes
notes: Event date: 21 August 1944 (Stacey, pp. 263-264). Event definition: The Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders, dug in at Magny on the Dives south-east of Trun, beat off a German attack with the help of very heavy artillery; the 9th Brigade meets the leading troops of the British 53rd Division about Trun in the morning. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 263: "Early in the morning there was a desperate German attack by infantry and tanks about the village of Magny, on the Dives south-east of Trun"; "Here The Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry Highlanders were dug in"; p. 264: "During the morning the leading troops of the 53rd British Division driving in from the west met the 9th Brigade about Trun". Location: Trun, Orne with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: Magny is a village a few miles south-east of Trun; the point is Trun. Location support: Stacey names Magny, south-east of Trun, and Trun itself (pp. 263-264). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: 9th Brigade patrols enter Rouen; Brigadier Rockingham is first into the main square
notes: Event date: 30 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 293). Event definition: After crossing the Seine at Elbeuf and moving north with the 9th Brigade leading from 29 August, the division sends patrols into Rouen on the afternoon of 30 August. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 293: "On the afternoon of 30 August the 9th Brigade pushed patrols into Rouen"; "Brigadier Rockingham himself was first into the main square". Location: Rouen, Seine-Maritime with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names the main square of Rouen as reached by Brigadier Rockingham (p. 293). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: Operation Wellhit: assault on Boulogne after bombing, 8th and 9th Brigades attack at 09:55
notes: Event date: 17 September 1944 (Stacey, pp. 339-340). Event definition: D Day of Operation Wellhit: Bomber Command opens over Boulogne at 08:25, and the 8th Brigade on the right and the 9th Brigade on the left attack at H Hour 09:55, with 328 guns in support (p. 338). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 339: "At 8:25 a.m. on 17 September the first aircraft from Bomber Command appeared over Boulogne"; p. 340: "The 8th Infantry Brigade (Brigadier Blackader) attacked on the right, the 9th (Brigadier Rockingham) on the left. H Hour was 9:55 a.m.". Location: Boulogne-sur-Mer, Pas-de-Calais with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names Boulogne as the objective (pp. 338-340). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: German garrison of Boulogne surrenders: General Heim gives up to Brigadier Rockingham at 16:30
notes: Event date: 22 September 1944, 16:30 (Stacey, p. 343). Event definition: The last of the Boulogne garrison, in the Outreau peninsula, surrenders when General Heim yields to Brigadier Rockingham at 16:30; Fort de la Creche had surrendered at 07:50 and the North Shore had taken Wimereux the same day. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 343: "ended on the afternoon of 22 September in the Outreau peninsula"; "General Heim surrendered to Brigadier Rockingham at 4:30 p.m."; "Six days were consumed in the operations against Boulogne". Location: Boulogne-sur-Mer, Pas-de-Calais with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the surrender took place on the Outreau peninsula south of the harbour; the point is Boulogne and stands for the area. Location support: Stacey names the Outreau peninsula and Le Portel for the last fighting (p. 343). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: Operation Undergo: division attacks the western defences of Calais at 10:15 after the bombing
notes: Event date: 25 September 1944, 10:15 (Stacey, p. 349). Event definition: Directly after the aerial bombardment the division advances against the western defences of Calais, the 8th Brigade attacking the Cape Blanc Nez and Noires Mottes defences on the left (p. 349). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 349: "At 10:15 a.m. on 25 September, immediately following the aerial bombardment"; "3rd Division's veterans advanced against the western defences of Calais". Location: Calais, Pas-de-Calais with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names Calais and its western defences as the objective (p. 349). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: All resistance in Calais ends by 09:00 after the Canadian Scottish and Regina Rifles finish mopping up
notes: Event date: 1 October 1944, 09:00 (Stacey, p. 352). Event definition: Scattered fighting continues through the night after the surrender ceremony and by 09:00 on 1 October all resistance in Calais has ceased, about 7500 prisoners having been taken (p. 352); the Canadian Scottish and The Regina Rifle Regiment finish mopping up (p. 393). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 352: "by nine o'clock on the morning of"; "1 October all resistance had ceased in Calais"; p. 393: "On 1 October the Canadian Scottish and The Regina Rifle Regiment finished mopping up the defenders of Calais". Location: Calais, Pas-de-Calais with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names the city of Calais (p. 352). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: Operation Switchback: 7th Brigade assaults across the Leopold Canal at 05:30 behind Wasp flamethrowers
notes: Event date: 6 October 1944 (Stacey, p. 393). Event definition: The division, moved up about 90 miles from Calais, assaults across the Leopold Canal at first light: 27 Wasp flamethrowers sear the north bank along the 7th Brigade front east of Strooibrug before the assault companies cross in boats; the 8th Brigade is to pass through the bridgehead. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 393: "Early on 6 October, having moved up some 90 miles, they assaulted across the Leopold Canal"; "At about 5:30 on the cold morning of 6 October, 27 Wasps went into action along the 7th Brigade front east of Strooibrug". Location: Leopold Canal (Leopoldkanaal), East Flanders with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the canal is long and Strooibrug is a hamlet on it; the point is a point on the canal near it, with a wide precision. Location support: Stacey names the Leopold Canal and Strooibrug (p. 393). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: 9th Brigade lands from Buffaloes on beaches east of Hoofdplaat about 02:00 behind the Leopold line
notes: Event date: 9 October 1944, about 02:00 (Stacey, p. 396). Event definition: The 9th Brigade, carried in two columns of 48 Buffaloes from Terneuzen, lands unopposed on Green Beach, a couple of miles east of Hoofdplaat (North Nova Scotia Highlanders), and Amber Beach, nearer the Braakman (Highland Light Infantry), behind the German Leopold Canal line. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 396: "The actual landing took place, then, in the early hours of 9 October"; "a couple of miles east of Hoofdplaat"; "The landing was set for 2:00 a.m.". Location: Hoofdplaat, Zeeland with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the beaches lie a couple of miles east of the village; the point is the village. Location support: Stacey names Hoofdplaat and the beaches near the Braakman (p. 396). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: Operation Switchback declared complete at 09:50 after the Breskens pocket is cleared
notes: Event date: 3 November 1944, 09:50 (Stacey, p. 400). Event definition: Switchback is virtually complete on 2 November, the 9th Brigade having cleared the area of Knocke and Heyst, the 7th the coastal strongpoints near Cadzand and the 8th the flooded area south of Knocke; at 09:50 on 3 November the operations log at division headquarters records Op Switchback now complete (p. 400). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 400: "The 9th Brigade had cleared the area of Knocke and Heyst"; "Op Switchback now complete". Location: Breskens, Zeeland (existing area place PL0569) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the existing area place for the Breskens pocket. Location support: Stacey dates the end of the operation by the log entry at division headquarters (p. 400); the pocket is the area between the Leopold Canal and the Scheldt. Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).

current_activity: Relieves the 82nd Airborne Division at midnight 12-13 November and holds the front east of Nijmegen
notes: Event date: 13 November 1944, midnight 12-13 (Stacey, p. 430). Event definition: The 82nd U.S. Airborne Division, under II Canadian Corps for a few days, is relieved at midnight 12-13 November by the 3rd Canadian Division, which holds the corps front east of Nijmegen. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 430: "when it was relieved by the 3rd Canadian Division"; "the 3rd Canadian east of Nijmegen". Location: Nijmegen, Gelderland with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the front is a line east of the city; the point is the city and stands for it. Location support: Stacey places the division east of Nijmegen (p. 430). Commander: Maj.-Gen. D. C. Spry (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 666: 18 Aug. 44 to 22 Mar. 45).
